Empirical Research Plan  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
1. Identification Strategy  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Method: Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) combined with a “difference-in-difference-in-differences’’ (DDD) interaction between treatment and a continuous measure of product-market competition.

Rationale  
• The 30 anti-takeover Business Combination (BC) laws were enacted at different times across states and were triggered largely by idiosyncratic takeover threats; they therefore provide plausibly exogenous shocks to the intensity of the external governance mechanism for incorporated firms.  
• The key research question is whether the effect of weakened governance (BC law passage) is heterogeneous across industries that differ in competitive pressure. This is naturally captured by interacting the DID treatment indicator with an ex-ante competition measure (HHI, Lerner index, etc.).  
• Panel data (1976-1995) and multiple pre- and post-periods allow for dynamic/event-study checks of the parallel-trends assumption.  
• The staggered adoption setting is now well understood; we will use stacked-DID or sun-and-Abraham estimators to avoid bias from heterogeneous treatment effects.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
2. Treatment and Control  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Treatment variable  
Treated = 1 for firm-years in which the firm’s state of incorporation has an active BC law in year t; 0 otherwise.

Control group  
Firms incorporated in states that have not yet passed a BC law in year t serve as contemporaneous controls. After adoption, those same firms can serve as their own controls in the pre-period (DID).

Treatment timing / event date  
• Statutory effective date of each state’s BC law (primary).  
• Newspaper “first mention’’ date as an alternate event window for announcement-based robustness checks.  
We code Post_st = 1 starting in the first full fiscal year after the law’s effective date (to avoid partial-year contamination).

Competition measure  
Comp_i = −HHI (so higher values = more competition) or, in robustness, decile dummies.  
Main interaction: Treated_st × Post_t × Comp_i (continuous) or Treated_st × Post_t for high- vs. low-competition subsamples.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
A1. Parallel Trends: Absent BC laws, operating-performance trajectories of treated and control firms would have evolved similarly, conditional on fixed effects and controls.  
Plausibility: States enacted BC laws due to firm-specific takeover threats rather than macro-economic conditions that would jointly affect all incorporated firms; we can visually and statistically test for pre-trends.

A2. No Spillovers (SUTVA): A BC law in state s affects only firms incorporated in s.  
Plausibility: Incorporation is sticky; a Delaware law does not directly constrain a Texas-incorporated firm. Product-market rivalry across states could generate minor spillovers; we will later show robustness restricting to single-state industries.

A3. Exogeneity of Competition Measure: Industry HHI is predetermined relative to law timing.  
Plausibility: HHIs are measured using lagged sales (t−1) and are largely driven by long-run industry structure; nonetheless, we re-compute HHIs excluding the firm i and using only pre-1980 data.

A4. Stable Composition: No systematic re-incorporation driven by anticipating BC laws.  
Plausibility: Re-incorporation is legally costly; we will verify low migration rates and, if necessary, instrument using incorporation state at least 5 years pre-law.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
T1. Differential pre-trends (violation of A1).  
Mitigation:  
• Include firm and state-year fixed effects plus state-specific linear trends.  
• Event-study plot (−6 to +6 years) using the Sun & Abraham (2020) estimator to document flat pre-coefficients.

T2. Simultaneous enactment of other state policies (e.g., poison-pill enabling statutes) correlated with BC laws.  
Mitigation:  
• Control for other AT laws (constituency statutes, control-share laws) with separate treatment dummies.  
• Drop states with overlapping statute introductions in sensitivity tests.

T3. Measurement error in HHI leading to attenuation bias in the interaction term.  
Mitigation:  
• Use multiple competition proxies (asset-based HHI, Lerner index, import penetration).  
• Instrument continuous HHI with lagged Census-based HHI (IV-DDD robustness).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
```r
# ---------- 0. Packages ----------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high‐dim FE models
library(did)         # Callaway–Sant’Anna / Sun–Abraham
library(readr)

# ---------- 1. Load & Merge ----------
comp <- fread("compustat_1976_1995.csv")        # firm‐year data
bc   <- fread("bc_law_dates.csv")               # state, eff_date, ann_date
hhi  <- fread("industry_hhi.csv")               # 3-digit SIC HHIs by year
state_panel <- fread("state_controls.csv")      # other AT laws

# Merge by gvkey‐year
dat <- merge(comp, hhi,  by = c("sic3","fyear"))
dat <- merge(dat, bc,   by = c("inc_state"), all.x = TRUE)
dat <- merge(dat, state_panel, by = c("inc_state","fyear"), all.x = TRUE)

# ---------- 2. Variable Construction ----------
dat[, post  := as.integer(fyear >= eff_year)]                # 1 if after BC law
dat[, treat := as.integer(!is.na(eff_year))]                 # ever treated dummy
dat[, comp_hhi := -hhi_sales]                                # higher = more comp
dat[, comp_decile := cut(comp_hhi, quantile(comp_hhi, probs=0:10/10,na.rm=TRUE),
                         include.lowest=TRUE, labels=FALSE)]

# Interaction
dat[, treat_post := treat * post]
dat[, int_comp   := treat_post * comp_hhi]

# ---------- 3. Main Specification ----------
# Sun & Abraham stacked estimator (allow for staggered)
sa <- sunab(dat$eff_year, dat$fyear, ref.p = -1)             # -1 = last pre
mod_main <- feols( roa ~ sunab(eff_year,fyear) * comp_hhi +
                   size + leverage + age + industry_fe, 
                   data = dat,
                   cluster = ~inc_state)

# summary(mod_main)

# ---------- 4. Classic 2×2 DID for simplest illustration ----------
mod_simple <- feols(roa ~ treat_post * comp_hhi + 
                    size + leverage + age + i(fyear) + i(gvkey),
                    data = dat, cluster = ~inc_state)

# ---------- 5. Robustness: alternative competition measure ----------
mod_alt <- feols(roa ~ treat_post * lerner + controls,
                 data = dat, cluster = ~inc_state)

# ---------- 6. Event Study Plot ----------
es <- sunab(dat$eff_year, dat$fyear)
mod_es <- feols(roa ~ es + controls, data = dat, cluster = ~inc_state)
iplot(mod_es)   # pre‐/post-coefficients
```

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
6. Expected Results  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
Theory (Holmström & Tirole; Scharfstein) predicts that product-market competition disciplines managers by threatening market share and profits if they slack off, whereas weak competition allows agency problems to surface when external governance is blunted.

Therefore:  
• In concentrated (low-competition) industries, passage of a BC law should lower operating performance (ROA) significantly—e.g., −0.8 to −1.2 percentage points of assets relative to baseline.  
• In competitive industries, the coefficient on the triple interaction should be economically small and statistically indistinguishable from zero, implying competition substitutes for takeover discipline.

Additional outcomes:  
• SG&A/Assets and wages per employee should rise only in low-competition industries (quiet-life).  
• Capital expenditure and acquisition intensity may rise across all industries (empire-building), but more so where competition is weak.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  
C1: Pre-treatment parallel trends visually confirmed ………………… 1  
C2: No anticipatory effects (no pre-law coefficients ≠ 0) ………………… 1  
C3: No spillovers or interference across units ………………………………… 0.5  
C4: Correct treatment timing (effective date + full fiscal year) ……… 1  
C5: Robustness to alternative estimators & controls shown …………… 1  

Total = 4.5 / 5.
